---
title: "Independence"
---

Does learning that a retained token has lemma *ne* change the probability that it is annotated as an object? We compare

$$
\mathbb{P}(O)
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N).
$$

We compare those probabilities in the token table, derive the equivalent product criterion, and then separate event independence from mutual exclusivity and row-level independence.

Recall that [conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd#conditioning-as-rescaling)
reweights the sample space after restricting attention to a conditioning event,
while the [joint probability](joint-probability-of-events.qmd#the-four-joint-events)
of two [events](events.qmd) is the probability of their intersection within the
[declared sample space](possibilities-and-events.qmd#outcomes-and-the-sample-space).
Independence asks
whether that restriction changes the probability of the other event.

Events $B$ and $C$ are [**independent**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson05) exactly when

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, this condition is equivalent to

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Three objects must remain separate. **Event independence** concerns two sets
under one probability measure. **Row independence** concerns whether repeated
sampled outcomes supply independent information; shared sentences and
registers can violate it. **Causal independence** concerns interventions or a
causal model. Establishing or rejecting event independence in this table does
not settle either of the other questions.

```{r}
#| label: load-independence-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L)

is_ne <- as.logical(wh$ne_lemma)
is_object <- as.logical(wh$object)
p_ne <- mean(is_ne)
p_object <- mean(is_object)
p_ne_object <- mean(is_ne & is_object)
p_product <- p_ne * p_object
p_object_given_ne <- mean(is_object[is_ne])

stopifnot(
  p_ne > 0,
  isTRUE(all.equal(p_ne_object / p_ne, p_object_given_ne))
)

c(observed_joint = p_ne_object,
  product_of_marginals = p_product,
  object_marginal = p_object,
  object_given_ne = p_object_given_ne)
```

## The observed comparison

Under the empirical measure,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(N,O)
\neq
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(N)\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(O).
$$

The observed joint mass is `r round(p_ne_object, 3)`, while the product-of-marginals model assigns `r round(p_product, 3)`. Equivalently, the overall object probability is `r round(p_object, 3)`, whereas the object probability among *ne* tokens is `r round(p_object_given_ne, 3)`. Thus the two events are not independent in this finite extract.

## Why the characterizations are equivalent

Suppose $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$. If

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C),
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B).
\end{aligned}
$$

Conversely, if $\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B)$, the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
&=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
\end{aligned}
$$

## Observed mass and the independence model

The product of the empirical margins defines a comparison model:

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathrm{ind}}(b,c)
\equiv
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(b)\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(c).
$$

It preserves the observed margins and replaces the joint cells by their
products, thereby removing the observed association. The same linguistic table
supplies the marginal probabilities; the product operation constructs the
comparison model.

For each of the four cells, the independence-model expected count is

$$
e_{bc}=167\,\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(B=b)\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(C=c)
=\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{167}.
$$

Comparing these expected counts with the observed four-cell counts shows where
the product factorization reallocates mass; it does not require treating the
expected counts as new observations.

```{r}
#| label: plot-independence-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Observed joint probabilities and probabilities under the product-of-observed-marginals independence model."
observed <- as.data.frame(
  xtabs(~ ne_lemma + object, data = wh) / nrow(wh)
)
names(observed)[3] <- "probability"
observed$source <- "observed"

ne_margin <- prop.table(table(wh$ne_lemma))
object_margin <- prop.table(table(wh$object))
independent <- expand.grid(
  ne_lemma = names(ne_margin),
  object = names(object_margin),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
independent$probability <-
  as.numeric(ne_margin[independent$ne_lemma]) *
  as.numeric(object_margin[independent$object])
independent$source <- "independence model"

comparison <- rbind(observed, independent)
comparison$cell <- paste(
  ifelse(comparison$ne_lemma == 1, "ne", "other"),
  ifelse(comparison$object == 1, "obj", "nsubj"),
  sep = " × "
)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  sum(independent$probability),
  1
)))

ggplot(comparison,
       aes(cell, probability, shape = source, color = source)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, position = position_dodge(width = 0.35)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(observed = "grey30",
                                `independence model` = "#2C7FB8")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Joint probability",
       color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Independence is not mutual exclusivity

If two positive-probability events are mutually exclusive, then their joint probability is the impossible-event probability while their marginal product is positive. They are thus dependent. Independence means that conditioning does not change probability; mutual exclusivity means that co-occurrence is impossible.

Observed dependence also does not identify a causal relation. The association between lemma and dependency relation may reflect the syntactic and semantic distribution of the lemmas, the selected registers, sentence clustering, and annotation choices. The empirical table shows dependence in the represented extract and nothing stronger.

Independence is a property of events under a particular probability measure. Changing the corpus population or observation process may change that property.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute the observed and independence-model probabilities for the *kim*–`obj` cell.
2. Verify conditional invariance for each row of `independent` and its failure for the observed *ne* row.
3. Explain why the mutually exclusive *hangi* and *kim* events are not independent when both have positive probability.
4. Which source identifiers in `wh` would you retain in a later model of dependence beyond this descriptive table, and why?
5. Can the events be dependent even if rows were sampled independently? Can
   the events be independent while rows remain clustered by sentence?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The observed *kim*–`obj` probability is $3/167=0.017964$, whereas the product-of-marginals model assigns $(17/167)(116/167)=0.070709$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Under independence, both object conditionals equal 0.694611; observed *ne* tokens give $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)=112/147=0.761905$, so conditional invariance fails. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The mutually exclusive *hangi* and *kim* events have joint probability zero but a positive product of marginals, so they are dependent. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A later dependence model should retain `sentence_id` for sentence clustering, `register` and `split` for corpus structure, and the full observation key including `token_id` for token identity. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Yes to both. Event independence describes the within-row joint
   distribution, while row independence describes dependence across sampled
   outcomes; neither entails the other.

</details>

Event independence is the product factorization of two event probabilities.
It is neither mutual exclusivity nor a claim about row-wise or causal
independence. The [next chapter](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd)
maps these outcome events to numeric random variables while retaining the same
probability-space logic.
